1:
Everyone reads the question as an objection raised on the Jew's behalf. Barnes ties it directly to the preceding chapter, where an uncircumcised Gentile keeping the law was to be reckoned as circumcised; Robertson, rendering it literally as the overplus of the Jew, calls it a pertinent question after so stinging an indictment. Calvin explains why it had to be met: the glorying was foolish, but a real doubt remained about the design of circumcision, since the Lord would not have appointed a partition-wall had no benefit been intended, and it would be inconsistent to void a distinction of which God was the author. Theodoret puts the difficulty sharply — if pious men among the nations share the divine favour, to what good did God separate Israel? Henry sets it out as the first of four objections, that a levelling doctrine denies the Jews the prerogatives God himself had given a holy nation and a peculiar treasure. Clarke goes further and stages the whole passage as a dialogue, prefixing the speakers, so that the apostle gives his countryman leave to answer and defend himself.

The answer is that the advantage is real but not meritorious. Calvin concedes the praise to the sacrament while refusing the pride: regarded as men the Jews were on a level with others, and what made them eminent was the free mercy of God and not any worthiness of their own. Henry makes the same distinction practically — the door stands open to Gentile as well as Jew, but the Jews had a fairer way up to it, having the means of salvation without the monopoly of it. Theodoret answers by rehearsing a whole history, the choice of their ancestors, the deliverance from Egypt, the miracles that made them the wonder of nations, the law and the prophets, and then declines to enumerate, contenting himself with the law alone. Gill and Robertson both translate the phrase as covering every side and every angle.

Whether a list was begun and abandoned divides them. Ellicott takes the word as first in the first place and says a secondly was to follow but never comes, the Apostle being drawn away to other topics; Robertson observes only that Paul does not add to his first and singles out one privilege of many; Wesley says the remaining prerogatives do follow, later in the epistle. Calvin denies that it is a note of number at all, taking it for especially and citing three other passages where the word carries that sense, though he notes that some read an unfinished period. Ellicott also corrects the English, since the oracles are the object and not the subject: they were entrusted with them.

On the oracles themselves the comment runs in three directions. Barnes and Robertson supply the word's history — among the heathen a response of a god or an inspired priest, brief and often ambiguous, and the seat of such a response as well, then common in the Greek Old Testament, and after Philo used of any sacred writing. Barnes and Henry both dwell on the trust, Barnes noting that the verb is the ordinary one for confidence and that the confidence was not misplaced, Henry calling the Jews the library-keepers of the Christian church, faithful to their charge and losing not one iota of the letter. Clarke agrees they had a treasure with which no other part of the world was favoured, but adds that they most grievously abused it. Calvin draws the conclusion he wants: the advantage lies not in the naked sign but in the word attached to it, so that apart from the word no excellency remained, the people being first depositories and then dispensers — and he turns the point on his own readers, who receive that word with so much negligence, not to say disdain.
3:
The objection is heard as a covenant objection. Barnes states it as the Jewish belief that all Jews would be saved on the ground of the covenant, so that if any perished God had failed to keep his word; Clarke, still writing the passage as a dialogue, gives the same complaint to the Jew — shall God falsify the everlasting promise made to Abraham because some of the nation are bad men? Ellicott notes that Paul first reduces the objection to its limits, since it was not all but some who disbelieved, and Calvin hears deliberate understatement there: he might truly have said a great part of the nation had renounced the covenant, but softened it for Jewish ears. Gill draws the limit differently, denying that any disbelieved the Scriptures to be God's word, which were always received and constantly read, and referring the unbelief to disobedience and to the rejection of the Messiah.

Robertson keeps both senses of the verb open, to disbelieve and to be unfaithful to a trust, and sees no real objection to letting all three related words mean faithfulness rather than faith. Calvin presses the same way, arguing that the question is not whether human unbelief unsettles God's truth in itself but whether it blocks its effect toward men, and answering that the covenant kept its efficacy in the few who by continuing to believe never fell from its privileges. Theodoret answers from foreknowledge, that God knew of old who would keep his law and who would break it, so that unbelievers could not invalidate the mercies; Wesley answers in one clause, that the promises still hold to those who do believe.

On the reply itself the tone is nearly uniform. Gill and Barnes both treat it as a first principle rather than a conclusion — God is faithful whatever men are, and Barnes says any doctrine of his own implying otherwise ought to be abandoned on the spot, adding that a man who really held this could be neither a Universalist nor an infidel. Ellicott puts it as a courtroom figure, God's justice arraigned before a higher tribunal and completely acquitted. Robertson renders the imperative as a continuing state, let God go on being true, and notes that the verb of justification, used of God, must mean declared righteous rather than made righteous. Calvin claims more, that the faithfulness of God is so far from being cancelled by human perfidy that it shines out the more plainly, God being true not only in standing to his promises but in performing whatever he declares, and man false not only in breaking his word but in naturally shunning truth — the first half of which he calls the primary axiom of all Christian philosophy.

The quotation divides them on a point of translation. Ellicott observes that Paul follows the Greek version, which turns the last verb passive, so that it applies not to the sentence God passes but to the imagined trial of that sentence. Calvin agrees on the fact and disputes the merit: the Greek translators rendered it passively against the Prophet's meaning, and Paul followed them because their words answered his purpose even better, the apostles habitually quoting with a freer hand than the original and counting it enough to cite what suited the subject. Clarke reads the psalm through the history instead, David acknowledging his sin so that the promise about his house might be vindicated when the threatened sword fell, and draws the rule that a man who thinks the promise has failed him should examine his own ways. Ellicott alone stops over the difficulty underneath, that good is drawn out of evil by design without overriding the will; how freedom and omnipotence agree looks insoluble, but the alternative would destroy human society. Theodoret asks only what diminution God's glory could suffer if every soul alive were ungrateful.
5:
Everyone treats the question as ventriloquised. Calvin says Paul assumes the person of the ungodly and writes not according to the ungodly but according to man, since the mysteries of God are paradoxes to the flesh, which has audacity enough to assail what it cannot comprehend. Barnes hears reverence in the same clause and calls the wording as artful as the case allows; he also cools the next phrase, since the noun means simply punishment and carries no necessary idea of vengeance. Ellicott admires the persistence — a profound question the Apostle's keen intellect will not let go — while noting that raising it at all requires an apology. Robertson leaves the verb ambiguous between commending and proving, and observes from Tholuck that the rabbis used both these formulae, so Paul had not forgotten his training. Gill narrows the claim: unrighteousness illustrates God's righteousness only by accident, in the punishing of sin, the setting forth of Christ, and the keeping of promises despite the failings of God's own people, of which David is the pregnant proof.

The reply divides them on method. Calvin holds that Paul gives no direct answer but expresses abhorrence, weightier than a denial, and that the refutation is indirect, drawn from an office rather than bare power: since judging the world is God's own work, and he cannot deny himself, he cannot determine anything unjustly — an argument traced to Abraham pleading over Sodom. Barnes says instead that Paul meets it head on, though the fact is neither explained nor conceded, the force resting on a premise no Jew would dispute. Ellicott thinks propounding the question answer enough, and lines it up beside Butler's reply to the argument from necessity. Barnes adds an illustration: a murderer is condemned by the law and his own desert, not acquitted because his trial displays the judge's integrity or his execution secures the commonwealth.

Robertson notes that Paul then shifts to the first person from delicacy, transferring the charge to himself; Ellicott finds both nouns moving toward their moral sense, the lie being the deflection following unbelief. Calvin sees the same objection as before, broken off mid-sentence by indignation, the vocabulary changing while the matter stays the same. Barnes locates the flaw: the objector assumes his conduct tends of itself to God's glory, when the tendency runs the other way and the glory comes only from God's overruling of it — every lost sinner being an eternal monument of the truth of God. Wesley says the apostle does not deign to answer but cuts the objector short with a severe reproof; Theodoret calls the speech absurd, since not even the most unjust of men would punish those who had advanced his glory.

The slander is handled briskly. Gill turns it into a taunt — why stop there, why not say it outright — and Clarke has the Apostle answer that the impious sentiment follows from the objector's own reasoning and has been injuriously charged on those who preach free pardon without works. Robertson calls the sentence tangled, offers two ways of untying it, and finds it uncanny that the Jesuit maxim should be laid at Paul's door so early. Ellicott supplies the missing words and says the Apostle will not dally with such a perversion of the moral sense; the pretext was either Antinomian excess fastened on Paul's teaching or a Judaizing complaint that a man who openly breaks the Law yet claims to be right. Calvin answers it directly, since evil can of itself produce nothing but evil, and God's turning it to his glory is his own work and not man's; the way prescribed for glorifying him is obedience, and whoever leaps that boundary dishonours him. Barnes draws the rule that no man is answerable for inferences others draw from his doctrine, and that evil is never to be done for any good expected from it.
9:
The opening verb defeats the grammarians. Robertson lays out three attempts — a middle sense of excelling to one's own advantage, Lightfoot's passive are we excelled, Vaughan's are we preferred — and leaves it unsettled; Ellicott takes it as middle for active, unexampled but compelled by the context. Both deny any contradiction with the much every way of the opening: there the reference was to external advantages, here to real worth before God; Calvin reconciles them from the other side, privileges granted freely never having been the Jews' own. Calvin notices a tact in the pronouns, Paul praising in the third person and accusing in the first, to avoid offence. The next verb is forensic for Calvin and Robertson alike, a prior accusation lodged before the tribunal, and Ellicott prefers the marginal charged; under sin, Calvin adds, means justly held under the curse.

On the quotations the comment turns textual. Robertson calls it a chain of proof-texts and cites Rendel Harris on the collections Jews and early Christians kept ready; both he and Ellicott note that the compound passage was afterwards imported bodily into the Greek fourteenth psalm, and thence into the Vulgate and the Prayer Book, a specimen of the corruption such quoting produced. Calvin sees a change of method rather than of text: having used arguments to convict men of iniquity, Paul now reasons from authority, the strongest proof for Christians — whence a lesson for teachers, who may assert nothing they cannot confirm from Scripture. Chrysostom explains the delay: it was the turn of the righteousness by faith, but Paul does not yet venture, having an eye to the violence of the Jews, and brings in David to say at length what Isaiah said briefly, a curb to keep his hearers from bounding off.

How far the indictment reaches is the one real dispute. Barnes confines it: the point proved is the depravity of the Jews, not of everyone, and the passage should not be adduced as directly proving universal depravity; the closing words are absent from the Hebrew and should not be pressed to deny that a single pious man existed. Clarke reads it the other way, as true of every soul in his natural state, since God, who cannot be deceived, looked down and found none. Ellicott grades the quotations, the first general enough to be directly in point, the middle ones aimed at particular oppressors, the last at the wicked rather than all. Gill defends the wording, the Hebrew saying none doeth good, whence none is righteous follows.

The particulars are read as a descent. Barnes finds high solemnity in the Searcher of hearts making investigation, and takes understanding for a disposition of the heart rather than of the mind, so that not seeking God is proof of depravity. Gill concedes that the natural faculty survives and that men understand things natural and civil, though none as Adam did, but denies them spiritual knowledge; Calvin is more absolute, a man without the knowledge of God being empty whatever else he has learnt, the arts good but hollow without that groundwork. On the turning aside Gill allegorises a bankrupt turned out of house and home, and Clarke divides the fault, the Jews forsaking law and prophets and the Gentiles the law written on their hearts. For the next word Robertson and Clarke both give it the Hebrew sense of going sour like milk, Clarke seeing the whole mass thrown together to putrefy in heaps; Ellicott reads together as altogether. Calvin takes it morally, that they had put off every feeling of humanity, inhumanity following ignorance of God; Wesley says they profit neither themselves nor others; Cyril reaches the verse at the end of a descent from Cain through the flood and Sodom to the calf and the prophets who could not cure the disease; Henry warns that it fits many who call themselves Christians.
13:
The open sepulchre is read two ways. Barnes reports both — the grave open to receive all into destruction, so that the slanderer's throat swallows up everyone's peace, or the vapour rising from a grave, so that noisome words issue from his mouth — and prefers the first; Calvin calls the throat a gulf wide enough to swallow men whole, more than calling them man-eaters. Robertson takes the other, their words carrying the odour of a newly opened grave; Ellicott combines them into a pestiferous chasm yawning after its prey. Gill piles up reasons, voracity, stench, and the danger of an open grave. Wesley traces a progress instead, evil discourse rising from the heart through throat and tongue until the mouth is filled, and notes that poison lies under the lips where honey lies on them. Barnes and Ellicott both locate the venom in a bag beneath the serpent's tooth.

Clarke alone raises the textual question: these verses stand in the Greek version but not the Hebrew and are missing from the Alexandrian manuscript, so Paul evidently quoted the Greek — or gathered them from scattered places, later copyists importing the block back into their psalters from his text. Calvin works the other way, tracing each member to its original and marking where Paul follows the Greek, corrects its order by the Hebrew, or drops a word.

On the cursing there is little dispute. Barnes notes that the psalm has deceits where Paul has bitterness, and takes the word for harshness and cruelty; Ellicott glosses it as malignity, venom being supposed to lodge in the gall; Calvin makes the clauses opposite vices, these men blending poison with their flatteries when they speak fair and pouring out bitterness when they speak their minds. Gill enumerates its objects, God, good men and superiors alike, and takes the mouth's fulness for frequency, betraying what the heart is full of; Wesley divides it, the cursing against God and the bitterness against the neighbour.

The verses from Isaiah are handled as a condensation. Barnes says the apostle refers to the passage rather than quoting it, and Calvin adds that he abbreviated it, altered two words of the Greek and dropped innocent before blood, the picture being a ferocity so barbarous that it leaves waste behind it. Gill thinks the original points at the times of Manasseh, and reads the middle clause both ways, the ruin they work on others and the ruin their own broad way ends in. Barnes and Clarke agree that they destroy the peace of all they touch and neither have quiet nor let others live in it; Robertson notes that the word for destruction means a crushing, and that they leave a trail of woe wherever they go. Gill extends the ignorance from peace with God to peace of conscience, which men imagine must be earned by something of their own; Calvin says only that men habituated to violence no longer know how to act kindly, and Wesley that peace springs from righteousness.

All make the closing line the root of the rest. Calvin returns to his thesis, that every wickedness flows from disregard of God, whose fear is a bridle without which we feel at liberty for anything; Gill defines that fear positively, a reverential affection springing from a sense of divine goodness and opposed to pride, absent from the unregenerate; Ellicott notes that a subjective feeling is here treated as an external rule of life; Wesley adds that the love of God is further off still. Clarke calls them practical atheists and turns from the text to the wars of his own generation. Barnes closes with the method: the citations come from six places and different periods, prove the tendency of human nature rather than the state of any man now, and spare no faculty, tongue, mouth, feet and lips alike perverted, the whole a ruin to weep over.
19:
What law is meant is settled quickly. Clarke observes it cannot be the Pentateuch, since none of the quotations just made comes from it, and takes it for the Jewish writings generally or the moral rule given to Jews in Scripture and to Gentiles in their hearts. Gill rules out the law of nature, the civil law of nations, the ceremonial law and the books of Moses alike, settling on the moral law as it stands in the whole word of God. Calvin and Wesley take it for the Old Testament at large. Theodoret finds precision in the preposition, since Paul writes not that the law speaks concerning those under it but to them: it says much concerning Babylonians and Persians, yet addresses even those predictions to the Jews. Ellicott adds that the two verbs differ, the first covering what is said and the second its promulgation.

Calvin explains why the Jews needed the reminder: no less destitute of righteousness than the Gentiles, they covered themselves with the covenant and applied to the Gentiles whatever the law said against mankind. He therefore reads the closing clauses as aimed at Jews who thought themselves exempt; Barnes reads them the other way, taking the purpose clause back over the whole argument so that the conclusion is universal; Wesley restricts it to those who own the law's authority. The stopped mouth is forensic for all of them. Calvin takes it from a court where the accused, convicted by his own conscience, waits mute for sentence, condemned by his silence; Henry sees mouths stopped both ways, the justified by humble conviction and the condemned sent speechless away; Robertson remarks that stopping mouths is difficult, Paul addressing the hardest to convince. Barnes notes that the word for guilty belongs to the courts, implies the punishment is deserved, and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Ellicott prefers guilty to God, the dative naming who is owed the penalty; Theodoret guards the purpose clause, since God gave laws consulting for men's salvation.

What the works of the law are is the long dispute. Calvin reports the learned divided, some extending the phrase to the whole law and others to ceremonies alone, naming three ancient writers for the narrower view; he argues for the whole, since Paul names precisely the works which could conceivably justify, the law being what attaches a reward to works. Barnes and Wesley take the moral law to be meant, Barnes adding that the charge throughout has been of a heart unconformed, not merely a life. Ellicott generalises furthest, to works done in obedience to any law, since law as such cannot justify — it might if men could keep it, but none can be kept strictly. Theodoret divides the Mosaic injunctions instead, some agreeing with what nature knows, since men who never received the law knew murder and theft deserved punishment, others imposed for that time only, symbols which even when performed cannot make the doer just.

On the closing clause the note is uniform and the images various. Henry says the law opens our wound and is unlikely to be the remedy, since what is searching is not sanative. Clarke compares a straight edge, the only thing by which a line can be shown crooked; Ellicott says the law holds the mirror up to guilt without removing it. Barnes turns it to preaching, since the more closely the rule is applied the more it condemns, which is how a sinner looks elsewhere. Calvin argues that life and death do not flow from one fountain, granting that the law is in itself the way to salvation and only our corruption keeps it from being so; Robertson says the universal effect of law is rebellion, Wesley that it delivers from neither the guilt nor the power of sin, and Gill that the works meant are imperfect ones done by sinful men of themselves.
21:
Why the righteousness is called God's is not agreed. Calvin leaves it open between a righteousness which alone can stand before God and one which God in mercy confers, contending for neither; Barnes rules out any divine attribute, since an attribute is not produced by faith, and takes it for God's plan of regarding men as righteous; Ellicott renders it a righteousness of God, wrought out and bestowed by him. On the freedom from law, Calvin insists that law here means works and not its teaching, cited two clauses later as a witness, and calls confining it to ceremonies unsound and frigid; Barnes guards the other flank, that God has not abandoned his law, Christ having come to magnify it, and that only justification by personal obedience is excluded; Ellicott makes it independence of law altogether, and Robertson says the same while denying the doctrine is any discovery of Paul's.

The opening adverb is read as an epoch. Ellicott takes it for these latter days, history dividing into periods with the gospel succeeding the law, and reads the verb as a manifestation begun at Christ's appearing and still unfolding. Calvin allows either an adversative or a temporal sense and, taking the second, distinguishes two manifestations, the earlier by word and sacrament and the fuller brightness of the gospel now, so the righteousness was not hidden before Christ came. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley press the witness borne by law and prophets, Barnes taking the law here for the books of Moses and pointing to Abraham, Clarke to the rites of the one and the predictions of the other. Theodoret admires the economy, that Paul shows at once that the law had ended and consented to grace; Henry asks whether the wound is incurable and answers that another way is laid open.

On the genitive of faith there is unanimity, and one dissent about its office. Calvin, Barnes and Robertson take it as objective, faith of which Christ is the object rather than faith Christ had, Calvin calling it a Hebraism and Robertson refusing the subjective reading outright. Calvin then sorts the causes, mercy efficient, Christ meritorious, the word with faith instrumental, faith justifying as the instrument by which Christ is received; Barnes says the same more briefly. Gill goes further, denying faith even the instrumental role on God's side and refusing it any part in the matter of a justifying righteousness, since faith belongs to sanctification and is a man's own. Ellicott turns instead to what faith is, an intense attachment resting on an intellectual basis but moral in working, recasting the whole nature.

The doubled phrase divides them at the level of the text. Ellicott reports the second half wanting in the best manuscripts and would drop it; everyone else builds on it. Wesley and Theodoret assign the phrases to Jews and Gentiles; Barnes grants the doubling is not obviously purposeful, but suggests the first means the plan has reached all and the second that it must be applied, perhaps glancing at a robe laid over nakedness — Henry's image too, a crown and a robe put on rather than offered. Calvin treats the repetition as amplification; Robertson notes that the word for difference is used of distinguishing the notes of instruments. On the last clause Ellicott insists on the aorist, a past act whose effect continues, and rules out the future glory of the Second Coming for something conferrable now, God's favour and approval, as Barnes takes it too. Clarke lists three renderings before settling on the rule that none but the holy can enjoy that glory. Gill traces the sin to Adam and draws two consequences, that no difference remains among men by nature and that none has ground to despair; Henry gives the failure three directions and adds that the way of spotless innocency is blocked by a flaming sword.
24:
The doubled emphasis is noticed by everyone. Calvin says it might have been enough to oppose grace to merits, but lest we imagine a half kind of grace Paul repeats himself and claims the whole glory for God's mercy; Wesley says the same, no words could more absolutely exclude every consideration of our own obedience. Calvin then sorts the causes, mercy efficient, Christ meritorious, faith instrumental, the glory of God's justice final, calling the passage the most striking in Scripture on that righteousness. Gill defines the grace narrowly, not the Gospel nor grace infused into the heart, but the free favour as it stands in God's own heart. Barnes qualifies the freeness: it is free to us, who have no offering and no claim, but cost a price, Christ having purchased it with his blood. Ellicott notes the odd grammar of the participle, one account of which yields the sense that men fall short of the glory of God and in that very destitution are justified.

On the ransom the comment is united. Barnes traces the root to the price paid for a prisoner of war and denies the broader sense of bare deliverance here, since the price is named in the next verse. Robertson adds that the noun is common in the papyri as purchase-money for freeing slaves, and insists God did not set men right with nothing done about their sins. Ellicott analyses the notion into three, a bondage, a deliverance and an equivalent paid, and argues that the redemption is wrought objectively and cannot be reduced to a change in the sinner, while confessing that what an equivalent can mean as applied to God we do not know. Calvin uses the same point against those who make righteousness a quality in us, since what is bought is derived from another.

The great word divides them. Gill, Clarke and Theodoret all hear the mercy-seat, Gill noting that the Septuagint regularly uses this word for it, Theodoret restricting the title to Christ as man, since as God he speaks from the propitiatory. Barnes works through five correspondences with the ark, then rejects the identification, since Christ as a mercy-seat would be unintelligible, and settles on a sacrifice. Ellicott weighs both, dismisses the objection that Christ would be at once victim and covering, but prefers sacrifice, since a public setting forth suits ill with a thing hidden in the Holy of Holies. Robertson rejects the mercy-seat outright and follows the inscriptions in taking the word for a votive gift, the crucified Christ being the votive gift of divine love. On the verb, Barnes holds the context requires public exhibition rather than fore-ordination; Calvin sets out what follows from each and declines to decide, adding that God, apart from Christ, is always angry with us — hating not his own workmanship but the uncleanness that has put out his image.

Where the blood belongs is a smaller question. Ellicott and Robertson both detach it from faith and attach it to the setting forth; Barnes leaves the connection and explains that the offering is made but not applied without faith, blood among the Hebrews being the seat of life. On the declared righteousness Barnes again refuses an attribute and takes it for the plan of justifying sinners, while Wesley insists on the vindictive justice whose office is to punish sin, adding that if God was never offended the propitiation was needless and Christ died in vain. Of the sins passed over, Barnes confines them to the past lives of those justified and warns that referring them to former generations makes universal salvation hard to avoid; Wesley reads them as the sins antecedent to believing; Clarke extends them to whatever Jew and Gentile committed while God's forbearance lasted; Theodoret says God bore with sinners not aimlessly but while preparing this means of salvation.
26:
Barnes calls the double title the substance of the gospel: to forgive without an atonement would make the law's penalty a nullity, whereas God regards his law no less in pardoning than in punishing, unlike an executive who sets a sentence aside without compensation. He denies nevertheless that the Son bore the precise penalty, his sufferings being neither eternal nor attended with despair, only that they reached the same ends. Wesley presses the other way, that justice is kept inviolate only if punishment was really inflicted on the Saviour, every attribute being glorified and not one clouded. Robertson calls it the key phrase and says nowhere has Paul put the problem of God more acutely, since pronouncing the unrighteous righteous is unjust, yet mercy would not leave man to his fate. Clarke divides it evenly, justice requiring a sacrifice, mercy providing it.

Calvin and Ellicott both read the clause as two-sided. Calvin makes the first part God's being just not as one among many but as containing all fulness of righteousness, full praise being his only when he alone bears the name while the race stands condemned, and the second the communication of it, God not keeping his riches laid up but pouring them out. Ellicott traces the same double character through the Testaments: under the old, God was revealed as just and found no answering righteousness in man, so justice could only condemn; under the new, it is met by a righteousness in the believer which is not inherent but conferred. Calvin makes much of the note of time, what was known obscurely under shadows being manifested when the sun of righteousness rose; Gill calls the present dispensation its display.

On boasting the note is triumphant. Calvin says teaching would not have been enough and the Holy Spirit had to thunder to lay our loftiness prostrate, merit of congruity and of condignity alike annihilated rather than reduced. Gill inventories what is lost, the Jew's descent and law, the Gentile's philosophy and freewill. Robertson renders the verb as an effective aorist, completely shut out; Ellicott fixes the moment, boasting being excluded when the law of faith came in, the question being not which law but what kind; Theodoret notes the precision, not destroyed but excluded, having no place now. Clarke has the Apostle grant that the law of works stands as a rule of life while denying it any place in salvation. Calling faith a law troubles several: Calvin admits the name is given without strict correctness, the righteousness of faith having a law of its own which leaves works none; Theodoret defends it from the prophecy of a new covenant; Barnes takes law for an arrangement or economy, Wesley for the constitution which makes faith the condition of acceptance. Henry guards the other flank: believers are not left lawless, faith being a working grace and the law still a rule in the Mediator's hand.

The closing sentence is disputed at the first word. Ellicott reports the best authorities divided between therefore and for, prefers the second, since the exclusion of boasting is the consequence rather than the cause, and objects that the English suggests an inference where the Greek asserts — we hold, rather than we conclude; Robertson notes the same variant and renders the verb as a fixed opinion; Clarke keeps the inference. Calvin takes the proposition as incontrovertible and turns on those who allow justification by faith but not by faith alone; he also reconciles the apparent conflict with James, whose question is not how men attain righteousness before God but how they prove it to others. Wesley adds that faith justifies not as a work but as it receives Christ; Theodoret notes that Paul writes not that a Jew but that a man is justified; Barnes recalls Luther's calling this the article by which the church stands or falls, while insisting it leaves good works untouched.
29:
Calvin sets the question precisely: Paul asks not whether God created the Gentiles, which nobody disputed, but whether he meant to show himself their Saviour; and the title carries the mutual relationship of the covenant formula, God's choosing a peculiar people for a time having never annulled the common origin of a race formed in his image. Ellicott would insert an alternative particle, taking the question up from the last verse, where any man simply as man was said to be capable of justification. Barnes and Clarke argue from the equality of guilt, that a plan fitted to sinners has no special reference to Jews and that God, if disposed to show mercy at all, has no reason to prefer one nation. Gill notes what the Jews would not allow the Gentiles any interest in; Robertson remarks drily that they overlooked this then and some Christians do now.

The unity of God is made to carry the argument. Ellicott lays it out as a strict disjunction: a distinction between Jew and Gentile could hold only if there were more gods than one or a second way of justifying, and since neither is so, none remains; he reads the future tense as covering the whole Christian dispensation. Gill reasons the same way from the divine simplicity, that one God in nature and will cannot have two methods of grace without being divided. Theodoret puts it as providence, that the Maker of all cannot be careful for some and leave the rest uncared for.

The two prepositions divide them. Clarke calls it fanciful to load them with different meanings, both being understood in the same sense and the added article merely sharpening the second; Barnes agrees there is no difference and that both make faith the instrumental cause. Ellicott grants a slight distinction, instrument against means, the anarthrous noun being the more abstract, the quality of faith in a man, and the second faith as embodied in the gospel, though the two are almost convertible. Robertson keeps it sharper, one preposition marking source and the other intermediate agency, and notes that the opening particle is a rhetorical politeness used of what is beyond doubt. Calvin suspects irony, as though Paul offered the Jews the only difference they could have; but he reports a serious version too, that the Jews were born heirs of grace by a right transmitted from the fathers while to the Gentiles the covenant came from outside.

The last objection is answered before it is proved. Calvin explains why it arises at all, since the flesh suspects contrariety wherever law is set against faith, and recalls that our Lord himself was accused of aiming at the law's abrogation and had to protest that he came to fulfil it; he therefore takes the defence to cover the whole law universally. Barnes narrows it to the moral law and answers the charge of licentiousness in three steps: God honoured the law by refusing to pardon without an atonement, Christ magnified it in life and death, and the plan itself produces obedience, since nothing so moves a man against sin as seeing what it cost his best friend. Clarke divides the law instead, the Mosaic rites established because Christ accomplished what they demanded, the moral because faith works by love; he warns at length against the Antinomian inference, since he only is saved from his sins who has the law written on his heart. Wesley sums it in three, that authority, purity and end are all confirmed. Ellicott, against most commentators, treats the sentence as an isolated assertion drawing on conclusions Paul had reached privately, the detailed proof reserved for later; Robertson and Theodoret read it forward instead, to the next chapter, where Paul goes at once to the root and shows that Abraham's own righteousness was of faith.
